title: Ofcom on the Online Safety Act: progress, problems and what needs fixing
label: 15 September 2026 · Online Safety Act evidence session
summary: Ofcom’s online-safety leaders told the committee which parts of the 2023 Online Safety Act are running, what still needs doing, and where the law and enforcement tools are causing headaches. They gave examples of progress—mainly around age checks and some big companies making commitments—but also explained why harms persist: legal limits in the law (a ‘safe harbour’ that can block tougher action), technical issues like VPNs, challenges enforcing penalties against foreign sites, the need for proactive scanning technology, and the strain from new government measures like the proposed under‑16s social-media ban. All three witnesses urged targeted legal fixes and clearer powers to make the regime work faster and more effectively.

speakers.label: Mark Bunting
speakers.name: Mark Bunting
speakers.role: Director, Online Safety Strategy Delivery, Ofcom

chapters.title: What’s in force and the timetable
chapters.takeaway: Some duties from the 2023 Online Safety Act are already in force, the bulk of the rules for big services are due mid‑2027, and new government plans (like a social‑media ban for under‑16s) are adding work and need extra funding.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. To start, can you say which parts of the Online Safety Act are live and what still needs doing?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Broadly, Ofcom is juggling three things: finishing implementation of the Act, making companies comply, and preparing for new duties the Government has proposed like the under‑16s social‑media ban.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: There are three main parts of the law: rules on illegal harms, rules to protect children from some legal but harmful content, and extra duties for big, 'categorised' services—those big platforms that get special rules.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We brought the child-protection rules into force in early 2025. The categorised‑services duties were delayed by legal challenges, but we published the list of categorised services and a consultation is closing. We expect those duties to be in force around mid‑2027.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: The Government’s new plans—like the social‑media ban—mean extra work. We asked the Government for more money in July and are discussing funding and the order of tasks; without extra staff something will have to give.

chapters.title: Have things actually got safer?
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom says there are real changes—especially better age checks and fewer easy routes to porn for kids—but the overall effect on children’s lived experience is still early and mixed.

turns.speaker: Lord Storey
turns.text: Has the Act made children and adults safer online yet?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We’ve seen major change in some areas. In a recent business survey of 125 services, 76% had done a risk assessment, 44% said they’d made changes, and 59% said they’d substantially implemented requirements.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Age checks are the clearest win: big services like Reddit, X and Discord added age gates, and among top porn sites there’s been a big jump in age checks—three‑quarters of the top 100 now either check age or block UK access.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: But some big platforms used by children still don’t have full ways to reliably tell who is a child. You can change one part of a system but you need the whole system to work to protect children properly.

turns.speaker: Lord Storey
turns.text: The Children’s Commissioner said the Act made 'absolutely no difference'—do you accept that?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We share the frustration. The Act aims for big corporate culture change, which takes time. We’ve started that change, but it’s early days across many different types of services.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Has contact with the Children’s Commissioner’s panel of children shown any clear improvements in real life?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We’ve got some positive anecdotes and we run monitoring so we can measure real experience over time. But AI advances are also making some harms worse, so it’s complicated.

chapters.title: Enforcement: what Ofcom can and can’t do
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom has opened investigations and fined firms, but legal limits in the Act, foreign services with no UK assets, and court challenges make enforcement slow or hard in some cases.

turns.speaker: Baroness Elliott of Whitburn Bay
turns.text: People say you’re slow and reactive. Why is it hard to identify and tackle new harms quickly?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We can move fast when needed—we launched an investigation into Grok (an AI feature on X) within two weeks. But we operate in a very litigious environment: companies bring court challenges and appeals, which slows things down.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: From enforcement, we’ve opened six focused enforcement programmes and 40 formal investigations covering over 100 services, and imposed £7 million in penalties so far.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: Practical limits bite: many offending services are small, based overseas with no UK assets, and sometimes won’t pay fines. Getting judgments recognised abroad is hard.

turns.speaker: Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate
turns.text: So is the problem legal tools, or your willingness to use them?

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: We are using our powers and are getting tougher—starting to use senior‑management liability tools and pushing business disruption measures (that’s a court order to block or stop a service in the UK). But those tools have practical limits.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: For example, if a forum withdraws from the UK, the law only applies while it operates in the UK, so court orders become harder to use.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How much of the £7 million in penalties has actually been paid?

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: Most has not been paid yet; we had a payment this week. I’ll follow up with exact figures for the committee.

chapters.title: Gaps in the law and technical issues
chapters.takeaway: Two big sticking points are the 'safe harbour' in the law that can limit enforcement and the narrow rules about using proactive scanning tech—plus issues like VPNs and cross‑jurisdiction enforcement.

turns.speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross
turns.text: You’ve suggested the 'safe harbour' in the Act is a problem—what do you mean by that?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: The Act set codes of practice that, if companies follow them, mean they’re legally treated as compliant—this is the 'safe harbour' idea. The trouble is companies can follow the code yet still have risks that aren’t fixed, and then we have less scope to take enforcement.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: From enforcement, big platforms will argue they’ve met the code, even if harms continue. That limits our ability to push them to do more.

turns.speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross
turns.text: Would a duty of care—making companies legally responsible for preventing harm—be simpler to enforce?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: A duty of care is an option, but it needs careful design. Broad duties can be hard to enforce because words like 'reasonable steps' lead to long legal fights about what was reasonable.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fleet
turns.text: On suicide and self‑harm exposure, campaigners say little has changed. Why can’t you force platforms to use automated scanning tech to find and remove that content?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: That’s called 'proactive tech'—scanning uploads before users see them. It’s powerful, but intrusive on privacy and speech. The Act lets us require it only if we can show it meets high standards of accuracy and intrusiveness.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We’re consulting on making more use of proactive tech. We think the case is strong for some harms, but the law makes the bar fairly high because of privacy and freedom‑of‑expression risks.

turns.speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross
turns.text: What about VPNs—kids using virtual private networks to get round age checks? Should the law force platforms to block that?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: VPN use rose when age gates were introduced, but not to the extent that the law is being widely evaded. Banning VPNs would be a big political and technical move; it’s not for Ofcom to decide alone.

chapters.title: Practical fixes and final asks
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom wants targeted legal fixes: more practical business‑disruption powers, clearer duty to tackle assessed risks (a kind of duty of care), and stronger ability to require proactive scanning tech—plus proper funding for new Government measures.

turns.speaker: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town
turns.text: If culture change is slow, should you hit firms harder financially so it hurts and forces faster change?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Yes—boardroom incentives matter. Big fines and litigation make safety rise up the executive agenda, like happened with data protection over time. But fines go to the Treasury; they don’t fund Ofcom.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: The Meta US settlement focused on system design rather than single posts. Does that suggest the law should tackle system‑level features like how algorithms push content?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: The settlement covered features like consumption volume and time spent, which the Act didn’t bring in. That’s a policy decision for Government and Parliament, but it’s relevant to harms we care about.

turns.speaker: Lord Tarassenko
turns.text: Final quick round: one change each that would most help you?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: I’d seek a way to make companies more clearly responsible for mitigating all the risks they identify—so we can require follow‑through beyond the codes.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: Fix business disruption measures so they work in practice against services that withdraw or don’t pay fines—those are our strongest enforcement tools but practical problems stop us using them.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Give us clearer power to require proactive scanning tech for certain harms, so we can stop content reaching users in the first place rather than only reacting afterwards.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you—all helpful. Please send the committee the exact fines‑paid figures, more detail on suggested legal tweaks, and anything else that helps Parliament decide on improvements.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: We will. Thank you for the chance to explain the work and the limits we face.
